newsitem.title: TURKEY: Military-Islamist security row widens in Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Military-Islamist security row widens in Turkey.

text.p: A security row that pits the military against Turkey's former Islamist-led coalition widened on Thursday when a senior policeman defended the government's right to secretly monitor possible coup preparations.

"If there is preparation for a coup, it is the duty of the police to watch this. This is our legal right," the Radikal newspaper quoted the police force's deputy intelligence chief, Hanefi Avci, as saying.

The new government of Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz and the military chiefs have announced investigations into newspaper claims that a police intelligence unit directed an infiltration and surveillance operation against the army on orders from the former administration.
The accusations emerged after a military document leak was traced to a former policeman alleged to have been planted in naval intelligence to spy on the military, newspapers said.

The affair, dubbed the "Mole Scandal" by the Turkish media, follows months of feuding between the secularist military and the previous government, which collapsed last month under pressure from the anti-Islamist generals.

The army, self-declared guardians of Turkey's secularist order, accused Erbakan's government of encouraging Islamic extremism in a series of public warnings that sparked speculation that the generals were preparing a coup.

Newspapers say that Bulent Orakoglu, the former deputy head of intelligence at police headquarters, obtained sensitive military documents and quizzed a contact planted in naval intelligence on the likely loyalty of troops in any coup.

The Interior Ministry has begun investigating allegations that Orakoglu organised the phone-tapping of senior military leaders. Orakoglu, appointed this year by former interior minister Meral Aksener, has denied any wrongdoing.

He was removed from his duties last month and then posted to the United States by Aksener just days before the government of former prime minister Necmettin Erbakan lost power to an anti-Islamist alliance.
The latest allegations were made amid a backlash from the secularist establishment against Erbakan's Islamists and his conservative ally Tansu Ciller.
A Turkish prosecutor questioned Ciller's husband on Wednesday over corruption charges arising from his wife's term in government.
Anatolian news agency said that an Ankara public prosecutor quizzed Ozer Ciller for 90 minutes. "A statement was taken from Ozer Ciller regarding allegations in certain newspapers," it said.
Erbakan's Welfare Party is facing the prospect of closure in a constitutional court case alleging that the party threatened NATO member Turkey's secular system.
